title: India Wants Positive Ties With Bangladesh, Says MEA Amid Hasina Extradition Row
excerpt: New Delhi calls Hasina's extradition a legal matter, postpones the November 17-18 consular dialogue in Dhaka, and says other channels on trade, water and borders remain open.
body:
• India said on Friday it wants a "positive, constructive and forward-looking" relationship with Bangladesh, even as the fifth round of bilateral consular talks planned for November 17-18 in Dhaka was postponed to a mutually convenient date.
  • Asked about Dhaka's demand for Sheikh Hasina's extradition, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said: "Extradition is a legal matter and it will be dealt with accordingly," and declined to comment on her possible return.
  • Bangladesh High Commission press minister Saidur Rahman rejected a link between the postponement and Hasina's November 9 request for a passport and national ID, saying the decision preceded that request by at least four days.
  • The postponed dialogue was to cover revised travel arrangements, visas and repatriation — issues that affect travellers and families on both sides of the border.

India on Friday said it wants a positive relationship with Bangladesh despite renewed friction over former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, whose presence in New Delhi since August 2024 remains the central irritant between the two neighbours. The statement came as the fifth round of the India-Bangladesh Consular Dialogue, scheduled in Dhaka for November 17-18, was postponed.

Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed the postponement at a briefing in New Delhi on November 13. He said the next round, which will also take up matters relating to the Revised Travel Arrangement, would be held on a mutually convenient date, according to reports by Devdiscourse and The Business Standard.

"India desires a positive, constructive and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

Extradition: a legal matter, New Delhi says

Hasina fled Dhaka on August 5, 2024, after her government collapsed amid a student-led mass uprising, and has lived in India since. Bangladesh's current government, led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, has sought her extradition under the treaty between the two countries. Hasina has been sentenced to death in Bangladesh in a crimes against humanity case concerning killings during the July 2024 uprising, according to Asia Daily's account of the dispute.

Asked repeatedly about the extradition demand, Jaiswal kept India's position to one line. "Extradition is a legal matter and it will be dealt with accordingly," he said. Clarifying the remark, he added: "When I talked about the legal matter, it is about the extradition part of it. To the other part of your question, I have no comment to offer," The Business Standard reported. He also declined to comment on reports that India wanted Bangladesh to send a military aircraft to bring Hasina back, or that New Delhi sought assurances of an appeal and a fresh trial.

Bangladesh disputes why the talks were put off

The reason for the postponement is itself disputed. A diplomatic source linked it to tensions over Hasina's announced intention to return to Bangladesh in December, and over a November 9 request — made through representatives acting for her — for a fresh passport and national identity card from the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi.

Saidur Rahman, minister for press at the Bangladesh High Commission, rejected that connection. "I can state with certainty that the decision to postpone the dialogue was made at least four days before the request for a passport and national ID on behalf of Sheikh Hasina was submitted on November 9. This has absolutely nothing to do with any announcement regarding Sheikh Hasina's potential return to the country," he said, as reported by Asia Daily. Dhaka has ruled out issuing new travel documents to Hasina, and Bangladesh's foreign minister has said the government would pursue her return through an extradition or an acceptable prisoner exchange process.

Relations had already come under strain after Hasina took part in a virtual media interaction from New Delhi on August 5. Bangladesh's foreign ministry said it was outraged the event was allowed; India responded that it had neither organised the interaction nor endorsed her remarks.

What the delay actually affects

The consular dialogue, established in 2017, is a working channel — not a summit. Its rounds cover visa procedures, repatriation of detained citizens, fishermen's release, and mutual legal assistance. The fourth round was held in New Delhi in May 2024 and covered visa matters, repatriation and extradition cases under the Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty. The postponed Dhaka round would have been the first since Hasina's government fell.

Jaiswal said engagement continues through other mechanisms, with meetings held on trade, railways, water resources and border management, and that India "remains ready to discuss all matters and bilateral issues with Bangladesh through these existing mechanisms, including at the technical level." Tourist visa services for Bangladeshi nationals resumed in June after a prolonged suspension, and the two sides held a Joint Working Group on Trade meeting in October, their first in three years.

What happens next

No replacement date for the consular dialogue has been announced. The next tests are practical: agreeing a new date, handling travel and repatriation cases through existing channels, and an approaching deadline on shared rivers — the Ganga Water Treaty is due to expire in December. India's extradition decision, whenever it comes, will be announced as a legal outcome, not a political one — that, at least, is the position New Delhi repeated on Friday.
